name: Banc d'Arguin National Park
blurb: Seagrass flats, millions of wintering shorebirds, monk seals and dolphins.

tip.title: Thin the seagrass
tip.text: Seagrass shelters clams and feeds turtles. Cut Dwarf eelgrass by 60% and watch the clams, then the red knots, harriers and octopus that depend on them.

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage: Banc d'Arguin National Park

notes: The story and why it matters come from the Wikipedia articles listed below (Banc d'Arguin National Park, Mediterranean monk seal, Zostera noltii). Individual species and links have not been checked one by one. Feeding links that match a GloBI (Global Biotic Interactions) record are marked in the node details, with a link to the records. A few links were added from GloBI records.

nodes.desc: Strong light over shallow, clear water lets seagrass and algae grow across the broad flats.

nodes.name: Bacteria
nodes.desc: Break down dead seagrass, algae and animals, releasing nutrients back to the mud and water.
Drifting and mud-surface microalgae fuelled by upwelled nutrients; they feed fish, clams and crabs.
Adults graze mostly on seagrass and algae in shallow lagoons and bays. The species occurs at the site and is listed by the IUCN.
Schooling fish of shallow coastal waters feeding on algae and detritus. Mullet are the main prey of Atlantic humpback dolphins.
Small schooling fish that eats plankton and is a major food for larger fish, seabirds and marine mammals in upwelling waters.
Long-distance migrant that winters on West African flats and in winter eats mainly hard-shelled prey such as bivalves.

link_ideas.what: Over two million migrant shorebirds winter here

story: Banc d'Arguin National Park lies on Mauritania's coast between Nouakchott and Nouadhibou. Its mudflats host over two million migrant waders from northern Europe, Siberia and Greenland. Between 25,000 and 40,000 pairs of 15 species nest here, the largest water bird colonies in West Africa.
matters: Its intertidal flats shelter some of the most pristine seagrass beds on earth. Only a small indigenous community may fish in the park, with primitive tools and no motor boats.
